query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Phase‐selective recrystallization of the soft phase in eutectic high-entropy alloys will improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility by eliminating weak internal boundaries and enhancing strain partitioning.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous weak internal boundaries and limited ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled phase‐selective recrystallization process to selectively recrystallize the soft phase while retaining the continuous hard-phase skeleton.
generation.conditions: Processing parameters (temperature, time, and cooling rate) must be set to promote recrystallization of the soft phase without coarsening or degrading the hard-phase network; the intervention is planned for room-temperature tensile conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A microstructure in which a fully recrystallized soft phase is embedded in a continuous hard-phase network, minimizing weak boundaries that serve as crack initiation sites.
generation.mechanism: Selective recrystallization enhances the strain hardening capacity by ensuring efficient strain partitioning between a ductile, recrystallized soft phase and a strong, intact hard phase. This reduces stress concentration at internal boundaries, delaying microcrack initiation under tensile loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional processing, the phase-selectively recrystallized alloy should exhibit a significant increase in uniform tensile elongation (up to ≈35%) and higher true tensile stress (around 2 GPa) at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy processing that results in dual-phase lamellar colonies with weak internal boundaries leading to early microcrack initiation and brittle behavior under tensile load.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only if the processing conditions can achieve selective recrystallization of the soft phase without adversely affecting the hard phase. Over-processing or non-optimal control of temperature and time may promote detrimental grain coarsening or insufficient recrystallization.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing parameters required to achieve optimal phase-selective recrystallization and reproducibility in large-scale production remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set processed by conventional methods, and the other by applying the phase-selective recrystallization process. Perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on both sets and compare the tensile stress-strain behavior along with detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM).
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves to assess true stress and uniform elongation
Microstructural analysis to confirm selective recrystallization of the soft phase and the integrity of the hard phase
Fractographic evaluation to identify crack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the phase-selectively recrystallized samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and uniform ductility compared to the conventional samples, or if microstructural analysis fails to verify the formation of a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in a hard-phase network, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials.
